abel.name: Abel
abel.summary: The shepherd whose offering pleased God, killed out of envy by his brother Cain: the first murder, in Genesis 4.

abraham.name: Abraham
abraham.summary: The father of the Hebrew people, to whom God promised descendants as many as the stars. He is called obedient because he was ready to sacrifice his son Isaac when God asked (Genesis 22).

acheron.name: Acheron
acheron.summary: A river of the underworld in Greek and Roman myth, which Dante makes the boundary of Hell proper. The souls of the damned gather on its bank from all over the world, and Charon ferries them across.

achilles.name: Achilles
achilles.tagline: Greek hero of the Trojan War
achilles.summary: The greatest warrior among the Greeks at Troy and the hero of Homer's Iliad. Dante, who couldn't read Homer, knew him from Latin poets and from medieval retellings of the war, which made much of his love affairs.

adam.name: Adam
adam.summary: Whose disobedience in Eden brought sin and death into the world, in the Bible's account. Christ freed him first from Limbo. Dante talks with him in Paradiso 26.

adrian-v.name: Pope Adrian V
adrian-v.summary: Ottobono Fieschi, of a noble family of Genoa and nephew of Pope Innocent IV. He was a cardinal and papal diplomat for many years. Elected pope in July 1276, he died in August, before he could be crowned.

aeneas.name: Aeneas
aeneas.summary: A prince of Troy who escaped the burning city carrying his father, Anchises, and after years of wandering reached Italy, where his descendants founded Rome. In Book 6 of the Aeneid he visits the underworld alive, the model Dante has in mind for his own journey.

albert-of-habsburg.name: Albert of Habsburg
albert-of-habsburg.summary: Albert I, son of Rudolf of Habsburg, elected emperor but never crowned. Like his father he stayed in Germany and never came to Italy. He was murdered by his nephew in 1308.

albertus-magnus.name: Albert the Great
albertus-magnus.summary: Albertus Magnus, a German Dominican who taught at Paris and Cologne and wrote on almost every branch of knowledge. He did more than anyone to make the works of Aristotle available and acceptable to Christian Europe, and was the teacher of Thomas Aquinas.

alexander-the-great.name: Alexander the Great
alexander-the-great.summary: The Macedonian king who conquered the Persian empire and led his army as far as India before dying at 32. In the Middle Ages he was the hero of a mass of legends and marvel stories, far more widely read than the histories.

anaxagoras.name: Anaxagoras
anaxagoras.summary: He taught that Mind sets the universe in order, and that the sun is a fiery stone, which got him tried in Athens for impiety.

anchises.name: Anchises
anchises.summary: A Trojan prince, loved by the goddess Venus, who bore him Aeneas. Aeneas carried him on his shoulders out of burning Troy. In Book 6 of Virgil's Aeneid, Aeneas goes down to the underworld and meets his father's shade in Elysium, where Anchises shows him the future of Rome.

angelic-orders.name: The orders of angels
angelic-orders.summary: Medieval theology sorted the angels into nine orders, grouped in threes. From highest to lowest: Seraphim, Cherubim, Thrones; Dominions, Virtues, Powers; Principalities, Archangels, Angels. The nearer an order is to God, the more it sees and loves. In Dante's universe each order turns one of the nine heavens.

angels.name: The angels
angels.tagline: Pure minds who move the heavens
angels.summary: Spirits without bodies, created by God, who see him directly. Medieval thinkers identified them with the Intelligences that philosophers said turn the heavenly spheres. Dante arranges them in nine orders, from the Seraphim down to the Angels, one order for each sphere (Paradiso 28).

anne.name: Saint Anne
anne.summary: The mother of Mary and grandmother of Jesus. She is not named in the Bible: her name and story come from early Christian legend. She was widely honored in the Middle Ages.

anselm.name: Anselm of Canterbury
anselm.summary: Born at Aosta in the Alps, a monk in Normandy and then archbishop of Canterbury. He is remembered for his argument for the existence of God from the very idea of God, and for Why God Became Man, on why the Incarnation was needed to make up for human sin.

antaeus.name: Antaeus
antaeus.summary: A son of Earth who lived in North Africa and fed on lions. He drew fresh strength from his mother whenever he touched the ground, until Hercules lifted him into the air and crushed him. Dante takes his story from Lucan's Pharsalia.

ante-purgatory.name: Ante-Purgatory
ante-purgatory.tagline: The lower slopes of the mountain
ante-purgatory.summary: The commentators' name for the shore and lower slopes of the mountain, below the gate of Purgatory proper. Souls who put off repentance until the end of their lives must wait here before they are let in to begin their cleansing. The prayers of the living can shorten the wait.

antenora.name: Antenora
antenora.tagline: Second zone of the ninth circle
antenora.summary: The second ring of the frozen lake of Cocytus, for those who betrayed their city, country or political party. It is named for Antenor, a Trojan elder who in medieval versions of the story betrayed Troy to the Greeks.

apollo.name: Apollo
apollo.tagline: Greek and Roman god of the sun and of poetry
apollo.summary: God of light, music, poetry and prophecy, whose oracle was at Delphi and whose sacred tree was the laurel. Dante often calls the sun by his name, and treats him as a figure for the true God's inspiration.

arachne.name: Arachne
arachne.summary: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, a young woman of Lydia so skilled at the loom that she challenged the goddess Minerva to a weaving contest. The goddess, enraged, destroyed her work and changed her into a spider. Dante shows her again as an example of pride punished (Purgatorio 12).

argus.name: Argus
argus.summary: In Greek myth, a herdsman with a hundred eyes, set by Juno to guard Io, a girl Jupiter had loved and turned into a cow. Mercury lulled all his eyes to sleep with a story and killed him. Juno put the eyes in the tail of her bird, the peacock. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Plato's student, whose works on logic, nature, ethics and politics were recovered in Latin translations, many by way of Arabic, and became the backbone of learning in Dante's time. Scholars called him simply "the Philosopher". Dante's ideas of sin and virtue lean on his Ethics throughout.

arius.name: Arius
arius.summary: A priest of Alexandria who taught that the Son was created by the Father and so was not God in the full sense. His teaching, Arianism, split the Church for generations. It was condemned in 325 at the Council of Nicaea, whose creed calls the Son "of one substance with the Father".

arnaut-daniel.name: Arnaut Daniel
arnaut-daniel.summary: A poet from Périgord in southern France, who wrote love songs in Provençal. He was a master of the difficult style, with rare rhymes and intricate forms, and he invented the sestina, a form Dante imitated. Dante thought him the best of the troubadours.

augustine.name: Saint Augustine
augustine.summary: Bishop of Hippo in North Africa and the most influential thinker of the Latin Church. His Confessions tell the story of his conversion, and his City of God answers the charge that Christianity had ruined Rome. Dante sees him seated in the Empyrean in Paradiso 32.

augustus.name: Augustus
augustus.summary: Caesar's adopted heir, who ended the civil wars and ruled Rome in peace. He was Virgil's patron. For Dante, the peace of his reign was the moment God chose for Christ to be born.

averroes.name: Averroes
averroes.summary: Ibn Rushd, a judge and physician of Córdoba whose commentaries on Aristotle were so thorough that Latin scholars called him simply "the Commentator". Some of his ideas were condemned in Paris in Dante's lifetime.

avicenna.name: Avicenna
avicenna.summary: Ibn Sina, whose Canon of Medicine was the main medical textbook of European universities in Dante's time. His philosophy also shaped Christian thinkers such as Thomas Aquinas.

beatrice.name: Beatrice
beatrice.summary: Beatrice Portinari, whom Dante loved from the age of nine and mourned in his early book, the Vita Nuova. In the Comedy she is a soul in Heaven who sends Virgil to rescue Dante, then guides him herself through Paradise.

belacqua.name: Belacqua
belacqua.summary: According to the early commentators, a Florentine who made parts for lutes and other stringed instruments, a friend of Dante's and a byword for laziness. Dante meets him in Purgatorio 4, sitting in the shade among those who put off repentance.

bellincione-berti.name: Bellincione Berti
bellincione-berti.summary: Head of the Ravignani, one of the great families of old Florence, and father of the "good Gualdrada" named in Inferno 16. In Paradiso 15 he is the model of the plain-living citizen of earlier days, who went about in a belt of leather and bone.

benedict.name: Saint Benedict
benedict.summary: Born at Norcia in central Italy, he left his studies in Rome to live as a hermit at Subiaco, then founded the monastery of Monte Cassino. His Rule, a plan for a life of prayer, reading and work under an abbot, became the pattern for monks across western Europe. Dante meets him among the contemplatives in Paradiso 22.

bernard-of-clairvaux.name: Saint Bernard of Clairvaux
bernard-of-clairvaux.summary: A Cistercian monk who founded the abbey of Clairvaux and became one of the most powerful churchmen of his century. He was famous for his writings on the love of God, for his life of contemplation and for his devotion to the Virgin Mary. Dante makes him the last of his three guides, in Paradiso 31–33.

bertran-de-born.name: Bertran de Born
bertran-de-born.summary: Lord of the castle of Hautefort in southwestern France and one of the great poets in Provençal, famous for his songs in praise of war. He was caught up in the quarrels of Henry II of England and his sons, and the old lives of the troubadours blame him for stirring them up. Dante names him elsewhere as the model poet of arms.

black-and-white-guelphs.name: Black and White Guelphs
black-and-white-guelphs.tagline: The two factions of Dante's Florence
black-and-white-guelphs.summary: By the 1290s the Guelph party ruled Florence, and it split in two. The Whites, led by the Cerchi family, wanted the city free of the pope's control. The Blacks, led by Corso Donati, looked to Pope Boniface VIII. Dante was a White. The Blacks seized the city in 1301 and banished their enemies, Dante among them.

bocca-degli-abati.name: Bocca degli Abati
bocca-degli-abati.summary: A Florentine nobleman who rode with the Guelph army at Montaperti in 1260 while secretly siding with the Ghibellines. According to the chroniclers, at the height of the battle he cut off the hand of the man carrying Florence's standard. The banner fell, the cavalry lost heart, and the army was routed.

boethius.name: Boethius
boethius.summary: A Roman senator and scholar who served the Gothic king Theodoric, was accused of treason, imprisoned and put to death. In prison he wrote the Consolation of Philosophy, in which Lady Philosophy teaches him that fortune's gifts are worthless beside the true good. It was among the most read books of the Middle Ages, and Dante says it consoled him after the death of Beatrice.

bologna.name: Bologna
bologna.summary: A rich city north of the Apennines, home of the oldest university in Europe, famous for its teachers of law. Dante knew the city and its dialect well and may have studied there.

bonaventure.name: Bonaventure
bonaventure.summary: Giovanni di Fidanza of Bagnoregio, near Orvieto, who taught theology at Paris, became head of the Franciscan order in 1257 and was made a cardinal in 1273. He wrote the official life of Francis, which Dante drew on. In the Heaven of the Sun he speaks for the second ring of the wise.

boniface-viii.name: Boniface VIII
boniface-viii.summary: Benedetto Caetani, who became pope when Celestine V resigned. He claimed power for the papacy over kings and cities, and his meddling in Florence led to Dante's exile. Dante treats him as his great enemy: he was still alive in 1300, but Inferno 19 shows a place in Hell being kept for him.

briareus.name: Briareus
briareus.summary: A giant of Greek myth with a hundred arms. In the version Dante follows, he fought with the giants against the gods and was struck down by Jupiter's thunderbolt. In Inferno 31 Dante asks to see him among the giants chained around the pit of Hell.

brunetto-latini.name: Brunetto Latini
brunetto-latini.summary: A notary who became one of the leading public men of Florence, and the city's great teacher of rhetoric and civic life. Exiled in France for some years, he wrote there an encyclopedia in French, the Treasure, and also a shorter poem in Italian, the Tesoretto. Dante honors him as the mentor of his youth.

brutus.name: Brutus
brutus.summary: Lucius Junius Brutus led the revolt that drove the last king, Tarquin, out of Rome around 509 BC and became one of the Republic's first two consuls. He is not the later Brutus who killed Caesar: that Brutus is in Lucifer's mouth, in Inferno 34.

bryson.name: Bryson
bryson.summary: An ancient Greek thinker who tried to square the circle, that is, to construct a square with exactly the area of a given circle. Aristotle criticized his method as unsound.

buonconte-da-montefeltro.name: Buonconte da Montefeltro
buonconte-da-montefeltro.summary: Son of Guido da Montefeltro, the soldier turned friar whom Dante meets among the false counselors in Inferno 27. Buonconte was a leader of the Ghibellines of Arezzo and was killed fighting the Florentines at the battle of Campaldino in 1289. His body was never found.

buondelmonte.name: Buondelmonte
buondelmonte.summary: Buondelmonte de' Buondelmonti, a young Florentine noble who broke his promise to marry a girl of the Amidei family and married another. The Amidei and their allies killed him on Easter morning by the Ponte Vecchio. Florentines traced the division of their city into Guelphs and Ghibellines to this murder.

cacciaguida.name: Cacciaguida
cacciaguida.summary: A Florentine of the 12th century, the earliest ancestor Dante names. Almost everything known of him comes from the poem: he was knighted by the emperor, followed him on crusade and died fighting. He greets Dante in the Heaven of Mars, and their meeting, in Paradiso 15–17, is the center of the Paradiso.

cain.name: Cain
cain.summary: The first murderer. In Genesis he kills his brother Abel out of envy, because God accepted Abel's offering and not his, and is condemned to wander the earth. The zone of Hell's lowest circle that holds traitors to their kin is named Caina after him (Inferno 32).

caina.name: Caina
caina.tagline: Where traitors to family are punished
caina.summary: The first of the four zones of the frozen lake at the bottom of Hell, the ninth circle. It holds those who betrayed their own kin, and is named for Cain, who killed his brother Abel. Dante reaches it in Inferno 32.

camilla.name: Camilla
camilla.summary: A fierce young warrior of the Volsci, raised in the wild and dedicated to the goddess Diana. She fought against Aeneas and the Trojans and was killed by a spear in Book 11 of the Aeneid.

cangrande-della-scala.name: Cangrande della Scala
cangrande-della-scala.summary: The greatest of the della Scala lords of Verona, a soldier who became the leader of the Ghibellines in northern Italy. He was Dante's host and patron during the later years of his exile. Many readers think he is the Greyhound foretold in Inferno 1.

capaneus.name: Capaneus
capaneus.tagline: One of the Seven against Thebes
capaneus.summary: A huge and godless warrior, one of the seven kings who attacked the Greek city of Thebes. In the Thebaid of the Roman poet Statius he climbs the city wall and dares Jupiter himself to stop him, and the god kills him with a thunderbolt. For Dante he is the type of the blasphemer.

capocchio.name: Capocchio
capocchio.summary: An alchemist burned alive at Siena in 1293. Early commentators call him a Florentine, or a Sienese, and say that he and Dante had known each other as students and that he was a brilliant mimic. Dante places him among the falsifiers in the last ditch of Malebolge.

cardinal-virtues.name: The cardinal virtues
cardinal-virtues.summary: The four virtues of the good life as ancient philosophy defined them, open to all people by reason, with or without faith. Christian teaching kept them beside the three theological virtues. Prudence, the practical wisdom that guides the others, was counted first.

casella.name: Casella
casella.summary: A singer and composer, from Florence or perhaps Pistoia, who died not long before 1300. Almost nothing is known of him beyond what Dante says in Purgatorio 2: that they were friends, and that his singing of love songs used to calm all Dante's cares.

cassius.name: Cassius
cassius.summary: Gaius Cassius Longinus, a Roman senator and general who planned the murder of Julius Caesar in 44 BC together with Brutus. He killed himself at Philippi two years later, when the conspirators' army was beaten.

cato.name: Cato
cato.summary: Cato the Younger, a Roman senator known for strict virtue, who fought for the Republic against Julius Caesar. After Caesar's victory he killed himself at Utica in North Africa rather than live under one man's rule. Dante, surprisingly, makes this pagan suicide the guardian of the shores of Purgatory.

cavalcante-de-cavalcanti.name: Cavalcante de' Cavalcanti
cavalcante-de-cavalcanti.summary: A wealthy Guelph of Florence and the father of the poet Guido Cavalcanti, Dante's close friend. He had a reputation as an Epicurean, one who did not believe the soul outlives the body.

celestial-rose.name: The celestial rose
celestial-rose.summary: The form in which Dante sees all the saved in the Empyrean: a vast white rose, each petal a seat, rising in rings like an amphitheater around a lake of God's light. Angels fly between the petals and God like bees. It is described in Paradiso 30–32.

celestine-v.name: Celestine V
celestine-v.summary: Pietro da Morrone, an aged hermit elected pope in 1294 after the papacy had stood empty for two years. Overwhelmed by the office, he resigned within five months. His successor, Boniface VIII, kept him confined until his death in 1296. The Church made him a saint in 1313.

centaurs.name: The Centaurs
centaurs.summary: A wild race of Greek myth, human to the waist and horse below, known for drunkenness and violence. Their most famous story is the battle they started at the wedding feast of the Lapiths. Dante makes them the guards of the river of blood.

cerberus.name: Cerberus
cerberus.summary: The monstrous hound that guards the entrance to the land of the dead in Greek and Roman myth. In the Aeneid he blocks the way of Aeneas and his guide. Dante makes him the guardian and tormentor of the gluttons in the third circle.

charity.name: Charity
charity.summary: The highest of the three theological virtues, with faith and hope. It means loving God above everything, and loving other people and all creation for God's sake. For Dante every good act comes from love rightly aimed, and every sin from love gone wrong.

charlemagne.name: Charlemagne
charlemagne.tagline: King of the Franks and emperor, died 814
charlemagne.summary: Ruler of most of western Europe, crowned emperor in Rome in the year 800. Medieval legend and song made him the champion of Christendom against the Saracens, surrounded by his twelve peers. Dante places him in Heaven among the warriors of the faith.

charles-ii-of-anjou.name: Charles II of Anjou
charles-ii-of-anjou.summary: Son of Charles of Anjou, known as Charles the Lame. He ruled southern Italy from Naples and led the Guelph cause there. Dante has little good to say of him, and attacks him in several places as a weak and grasping king who sold his own daughter in marriage.

charles-martel.name: Charles Martel
charles-martel.summary: Charles Martel of Anjou, eldest son of Charles II of Naples and heir to Naples and Provence. Through his mother he also held the title of king of Hungary. He visited Florence in 1294, where Dante seems to have met and liked him, and died the next year at twenty-four. He is not the Frankish Charles Martel of the 8th century.

charles-of-anjou.name: Charles of Anjou
charles-of-anjou.summary: Brother of King Louis IX of France. Invited into Italy by the pope, he conquered the kingdom of Sicily, defeating Manfred at Benevento in 1266 and Conradin at Tagliacozzo in 1268, and became the leader of the Guelph cause in Italy. He lost the island of Sicily in the revolt of 1282 known as the Sicilian Vespers. Dante places him among the princes in Purgatorio 7.

charles-of-valois.name: Charles of Valois
charles-of-valois.summary: The brother of King Philip the Fair of France. Pope Boniface VIII sent him to Florence in 1301 as a peacemaker. He instead helped the Black Guelphs seize the city, which led to Dante's exile.

charon.name: Charon
charon.summary: In Greek and Roman myth, the old boatman who carries the souls of the dead across the river into the underworld. Dante takes him from Book 6 of the Aeneid and sets him on the Acheron.

chiron.name: Chiron
chiron.summary: Unlike the other centaurs he was gentle and learned, skilled in medicine and music. He was the teacher of Achilles and of other Greek heroes. Dante makes him the leader of the centaurs who guard the violent.

cicero.name: Cicero
cicero.summary: Rome's greatest orator, and a philosopher whose Latin prose was the model for centuries. Dante, who called him Tully, wrote that Cicero's essay On Friendship helped console him after Beatrice died.

cimabue.name: Cimabue
cimabue.summary: The leading painter in Florence in the generation before Giotto, known for great painted crucifixes and altarpieces of the Virgin enthroned. Tradition makes him Giotto's teacher.

cincinnatus.name: Cincinnatus
cincinnatus.summary: Lucius Quinctius Cincinnatus, a Roman called from his plough in 458 BC to lead the state as dictator in an emergency. He defeated the enemy, laid down his power within days and went back to his farm. For the Romans, and for Dante, he was the pattern of selfless public service.

circe.name: Circe
circe.summary: A sorceress, daughter of the Sun, who lived on an island off the coast of Italy. In the Odyssey she turns Ulysses's men into swine, and he stays with her for a year. Ulysses mentions her when he tells Dante of his last voyage in Inferno 26.

clare-of-assisi.name: Clare of Assisi
clare-of-assisi.tagline: Saint and founder of the Poor Clares, 1194–1253
clare-of-assisi.summary: A noblewoman of Assisi who left her family in 1212 to follow Francis of Assisi in a life of poverty. She founded the order of nuns later called the Poor Clares, and was declared a saint two years after her death.

clement-v.name: Clement V
clement-v.summary: Bertrand de Got, a Gascon and archbishop of Bordeaux, elected pope with the backing of the king of France. He never went to Rome, and in 1309 he settled the papal court at Avignon, where it stayed for some seventy years. Dante also accuses him of betraying the emperor Henry VII, on whom Dante had set his hopes for Italy.

cleopatra.name: Cleopatra
cleopatra.summary: The last of the Ptolemies to rule Egypt, lover of Julius Caesar and then of Mark Antony. After Octavian, the future emperor Augustus, defeated her and Antony, she killed herself, by the bite of a snake according to tradition.

cocytus.name: Cocytus
cocytus.tagline: The frozen lake of the ninth circle
cocytus.summary: In classical myth the river of wailing. Dante makes it a lake of ice at the bottom of Hell, where traitors are frozen in four zones: traitors to family, to country, to guests, and to their lords. Lucifer stands fixed at its center (Inferno 32–34).

conrad-iii.name: Conrad III
conrad-iii.summary: The first ruler of the Hohenstaufen family. With Louis VII of France he led the Second Crusade (1147–1149), which failed. He was never actually crowned emperor, though Dante gives him the title.

constance-of-sicily.name: Constance of Sicily
constance-of-sicily.summary: Daughter of the Norman king Roger II and heiress to the kingdom of Sicily. She married the emperor Henry VI in 1186 and was the mother of Frederick II. A story current in Dante’s time, which historians do not accept, said she had been a nun and was taken from her convent to make the marriage.

constantine.name: Constantine
constantine.summary: The first Christian emperor, who ended the persecution of Christians and moved the capital of the empire east to Constantinople. The Middle Ages believed that he also gave the pope rule over Rome and the West, the so-called Donation of Constantine. Dante held that this gift ruined the Church by making it rich, yet he places Constantine in Heaven for his good intention (Paradiso 20).

cornelia.name: Cornelia
cornelia.summary: Probably the mother of the Gracchi, the reforming brothers Tiberius and Gaius, and Rome's model of the virtuous mother. She is praised again in Paradiso 15.

counts-guidi.name: The Counts Guidi
counts-guidi.tagline: Feudal lords of the Tuscan mountains
counts-guidi.summary: One of the most powerful noble families of medieval Tuscany, with castles in the Casentino, the upper valley of the Arno, and across the mountains in Romagna. The family split into several branches, some Guelph and some Ghibelline. Several of its members appear in the poem, and Dante was a guest of the family during his exile.

cunizza-da-romano.name: Cunizza da Romano
cunizza-da-romano.summary: Sister of the tyrant Ezzelino, famous in her day for her husbands and lovers, among them the troubadour Sordello. She spent her old age in Florence, where in 1265 she freed her family's serfs. Dante places her among the lovers in the Heaven of Venus.

currado-malaspina.name: Currado Malaspina
currado-malaspina.tagline: Lord in the Lunigiana, died about 1294
currado-malaspina.summary: Conrad Malaspina the younger, a marquis of the family that held the Lunigiana, the hill country between Tuscany and Liguria. The Malaspina were known for their generosity, and they sheltered Dante in 1306, early in his exile.

daedalus.name: Daedalus
daedalus.summary: The inventor who built the labyrinth of Crete for King Minos. Held prisoner on the island, he made wings of feathers and wax and flew away with his son Icarus, who flew too near the sun and fell into the sea. His name stands for supreme skill.

daniel.name: Daniel
daniel.summary: A young Jewish exile at the court of Babylon, in the biblical book that bears his name. He interprets the dreams of King Nebuchadnezzar, survives the lions' den, and has visions of God's throne and the end of time.

david.name: King David
david.summary: The shepherd boy who killed Goliath and became Israel's greatest king, held to be the author of the Psalms. Dante sees him carved dancing before the Ark in Purgatorio 10 and shining in the eye of the Eagle in Paradiso 20.

democritus.name: Democritus
democritus.summary: He taught that everything is made of tiny atoms colliding in empty space, so the world came to be by chance, not design: the view Dante singles out.

dido.name: Dido
dido.summary: The founder of Carthage in Virgil's Aeneid. A widow sworn to the memory of her husband, Sichaeus, she fell in love with Aeneas when he was shipwrecked on her coast. When he sailed away to Italy at the gods' command, she killed herself on a pyre.

diogenes.name: Diogenes
diogenes.summary: Probably Diogenes the Cynic, who scorned wealth and custom, lived in a large clay jar, and is said to have told Alexander the Great to step out of his sunlight.

dionysius-the-areopagite.name: Dionysius the Areopagite
dionysius-the-areopagite.summary: An Athenian judge converted by Paul's preaching (Acts 17). The Middle Ages believed he wrote the Celestial Hierarchy, the book that sorts the angels into nine orders, and that he learned it from Paul himself. The book was in fact written by an unknown author about 500. Dante follows its order of the angels in Paradiso 28.

dioscorides.name: Dioscorides
dioscorides.summary: A Greek doctor, said to have served in Nero's armies, whose Materia Medica described the healing "qualities" of some six hundred plants. It stayed the standard book of medicines for fifteen hundred years.

dis.name: Dis
dis.tagline: The walled city of lower Hell
dis.summary: Dis was a Roman name for Pluto, king of the underworld. Dante gives it to Lucifer, and to the iron-walled city that encloses the lower circles of Hell, from the sixth down. Inside are punished the sins of malice: heresy, violence, fraud and treachery.

dominic.name: Saint Dominic
dominic.summary: A Spanish priest who founded the Order of Preachers, friars vowed to poverty and trained in theology, to win back heretics by preaching and argument. His order produced the great university teachers of the 13th century. His life is told in Paradiso 12.

dominicans.name: The Dominicans
dominicans.summary: The Order of Preachers, founded by Dominic and approved by the pope in 1216. Its friars lived on alms like the Franciscans but were devoted above all to study and preaching, and they soon filled the universities. Thomas Aquinas was one of them.

donati.name: The Donati
donati.summary: An old noble family of Florence, neighbors of the Alighieri. Dante's wife, Gemma, was a Donati. Corso Donati led the Black Guelphs, who had Dante banished. Corso's brother Forese was Dante's friend and appears in Purgatorio 23–24, and their sister Piccarda in Paradiso 3.

donatus.name: Donatus
donatus.summary: Aelius Donatus, a teacher in Rome whose pupils included Saint Jerome. His Latin grammar was the first schoolbook of every medieval student.

eagle.name: The Eagle
eagle.tagline: Emblem of the empire and of justice
eagle.summary: The eagle was the bird of Jupiter, the standard of the Roman legions and the emblem of the empire, which Dante believed God had appointed to give the world justice. In the heaven of Jupiter the souls of just rulers join to form a great eagle of lights, which speaks with a single voice (Paradiso 18–20).

earthly-paradise.name: The Earthly Paradise
earthly-paradise.summary: The garden God made for Adam and Eve, which Dante sets on the summit of the mountain of Purgatory. It is a forest of unending spring, empty since the Fall. Souls who have finished their cleansing pass through it on the way to Heaven, recovering the innocence humanity lost.

electra.name: Electra
electra.tagline: Mother of the founder of Troy
electra.summary: Not Agamemnon's daughter of Greek tragedy, but the daughter of Atlas who bore Dardanus to Jupiter. Dardanus founded the line of Troy's kings, and through Aeneas the line of Rome.

elijah.name: Elijah
elijah.summary: A prophet of the Old Testament who, at the end of his life, was carried up to heaven in a chariot of fire (2 Kings 2). In the Gospels he appears with Moses beside Christ at the Transfiguration.

empedocles.name: Empedocles
empedocles.summary: He taught that the world is made of four elements, joined by Love and pulled apart by Strife. Virgil recalls the idea in Inferno 12. Legend says he threw himself into the crater of Mount Etna.

empyrean.name: The Empyrean
empyrean.summary: The heaven beyond the nine turning spheres of the planets and stars, outside space and time. It is pure light and love, the true home of God, the angels and all the blessed. Dante reaches it in Paradiso 30.

epicurus.name: Epicurus
epicurus.summary: He taught that the goal of life is pleasure, by which he meant peace of mind and freedom from pain and fear. He held that the soul is made of atoms and comes apart at death, so there is nothing after it to dread. Medieval writers knew him mostly at second hand and used his name for anyone who denied the afterlife.

erichtho.name: Erichtho
erichtho.summary: A sorceress in Lucan's epic, the Pharsalia. Before the battle between Caesar and Pompey, she forces the soul of a dead soldier back into its body so that it can foretell the outcome. For medieval readers she was the type of the witch who raises the dead.

euclid.name: Euclid
euclid.summary: Author of the Elements, which built geometry step by step from a few axioms. It was how geometry was taught for two thousand years.

eunoe.name: Eunoe
eunoe.summary: The second river of the Garden of Eden, and Dante's own invention. Its name is made from Greek words meaning "good mind". Its water restores the memory of every good deed, and souls drink it last, after Lethe, before rising to Heaven.

eve.name: Eve
eve.summary: In Genesis, the wife of Adam. Tempted by the serpent, she ate the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, which God had forbidden, and gave it to Adam. For this the two were driven out of the Garden of Eden, which Dante places at the top of the mountain of Purgatory.

ezekiel.name: Ezekiel
ezekiel.summary: A prophet among the Jews exiled to Babylon, and the author of the biblical book that bears his name. It opens with his vision of God's chariot-throne, carried by four winged living creatures.

ezzelino-da-romano.name: Ezzelino da Romano
ezzelino-da-romano.summary: Ghibelline lord of Verona, Padua and the lands around them, and son-in-law of the emperor Frederick II. His massacres and tortures made him the most feared man of his century, and legend called him a son of the devil. His sister Cunizza speaks of him in Paradiso 9.

farinata.name: Farinata degli Uberti
farinata.summary: Head of the Ghibelline party in Florence, the enemies of Dante's own Guelph ancestors. He helped win the battle of Montaperti in 1260, and afterwards stopped his allies from destroying Florence. Dante meets him among the heretics in Inferno 10.

fiesole.name: Fiesole
fiesole.summary: An ancient Etruscan town on the hills just north of Florence. Legend said the Romans destroyed it and founded Florence in the valley below, settling it with a mix of noble Romans and rough Fiesolans. Dante blames the city's quarrels on that mixed blood, and counts himself among the heirs of the Romans.

filippo-argenti.name: Filippo Argenti
filippo-argenti.summary: A member of the powerful Adimari family of Florence, known for his violent temper. Early commentators say he was nicknamed Argenti, "silver", because he had his horse shod with it. They also report bad blood between his family and Dante, in stories that can't be verified.

florence.name: Florence
florence.summary: A rich and fast-growing city republic in Tuscany, where Dante was born in 1265 and held office in 1300. It was torn by feuds between its parties, and in 1302 the winning faction banished him for life. His love for the city and his fury at it run through the whole poem.

folco-of-marseille.name: Folco of Marseille
folco-of-marseille.summary: Folquet de Marseille, a famous Provençal love poet who gave up the world, became a Cistercian monk and abbot, and in 1205 bishop of Toulouse. As bishop he was a fierce enemy of the Cathar heretics during the Albigensian Crusade, a side of him Dante does not mention.

forese-donati.name: Forese Donati
forese-donati.summary: A member of the powerful Donati family of Florence, and a friend of Dante in his youth. He was the brother of Corso Donati, leader of the Black Guelphs, and of Piccarda, and a distant kinsman of Dante's wife, Gemma Donati. He and Dante exchanged a series of comic, insulting sonnets that still survive.

fortune.name: Fortune
fortune.summary: To the Romans a fickle goddess, and to the Middle Ages a blind woman turning a wheel. Dante makes her an angel instead. God has appointed her to move wealth and power from person to person and nation to nation, by a plan no human mind can follow or resist.

francesca-da-rimini.name: Francesca da Rimini
francesca-da-rimini.summary: Daughter of Guido da Polenta, lord of Ravenna, married for political reasons to Gianciotto Malatesta of Rimini. She became the lover of his younger brother Paolo, and Gianciotto killed them both. The date is uncertain, and Dante's is the earliest account of the story: he was a young man when it happened.

francis-of-assisi.name: Francis of Assisi
francis-of-assisi.summary: A rich merchant's son from Assisi who gave up everything to live in poverty and preach. He founded the Franciscans, or Friars Minor, who wore a rough habit tied with a cord. Two years before his death he received the stigmata, the wounds of Christ. His life is told in Paradiso 11.

franciscans.name: The Franciscans
franciscans.summary: The Friars Minor, or "lesser brothers", founded by Francis of Assisi and approved by the pope in 1209 or 1210. They vowed to own nothing and wore a rough habit tied with a cord. By Dante's time the order was bitterly split between the Spirituals, who held to strict poverty, and those who wanted the rule relaxed.

frederick-barbarossa.name: Frederick Barbarossa
frederick-barbarossa.summary: Frederick I, called Barbarossa, "Redbeard", by the Italians. He fought for decades to impose imperial rule on the cities of northern Italy and destroyed Milan in 1162. He drowned on the way to the Third Crusade. He was the grandfather of Frederick II.

frederick-ii.name: Frederick II
frederick-ii.summary: Emperor and king of Sicily, called the wonder of the world for his learning. His court in southern Italy produced the first school of Italian poetry. He fought the popes for decades and was excommunicated more than once, and his enemies called him an unbeliever. His minister Pier della Vigna speaks in Inferno 13.

furies.name: The Furies
furies.summary: Three sisters of Greek and Roman myth, also called the Erinyes: Alecto, Megaera and Tisiphone. They have snakes for hair and hunt down the guilty, above all those who shed the blood of their own family. In Latin poetry they serve the rulers of the underworld.

gabriel.name: Gabriel
gabriel.summary: The angel sent to tell Mary that she would be the mother of Christ, as told in Luke's Gospel. His greeting, "Hail", begins the prayer Hail Mary.

galen.name: Galen
galen.summary: Doctor to emperors and to gladiators, whose writings on anatomy and the four humors governed European and Islamic medicine for over a thousand years.

geryon.name: Geryon
geryon.summary: In classical myth a giant with three bodies, killed by Hercules. Dante keeps only the name and invents a new creature: the face of an honest man, the paws of a beast, a serpent's painted body and a scorpion's sting in the tail. He is the image of fraud, and carries Dante and Virgil on his back down to the eighth circle.

giants.name: The Giants
giants.summary: In classical myth the Giants were sons of Earth who tried to storm Olympus and were struck down by Jove's thunderbolts at Phlegra. The Bible also speaks of giants on the earth in the early days (Genesis 6). Dante sets them around the pit that leads to the ninth circle: huge strength that rose in pride against heaven, now fixed in place.

giotto.name: Giotto
giotto.summary: The painter who gave figures weight, space and feeling, and so changed the course of European art. His frescoes in the Arena Chapel in Padua were painted about 1305. He was Dante's contemporary, and an old tradition makes the two friends.

giraut-de-bornelh.name: Giraut de Bornelh
giraut-de-bornelh.summary: A poet from the Limousin region of southern France, who wrote in Provençal. In his own time he was called the master of the troubadours, and he was known for poems of moral seriousness.

gregory-the-great.name: Gregory the Great
gregory-the-great.summary: Pope Gregory I, one of the great teachers of the early Church and a writer much read in the Middle Ages. A famous legend said that his prayers won salvation for the pagan emperor Trajan.

greyhound.name: The Greyhound
greyhound.summary: Virgil's prophecy of a leader who will drive greed out of the world. Dante never says who he means. The likeliest candidates are Cangrande della Scala, lord of Verona and Dante's patron in exile, and the emperor Henry VII; others think of a future pope, or of Christ's return.

griffin.name: The Griffin
griffin.summary: A legendary animal with the head and wings of an eagle and the body of a lion. In the procession at the top of Purgatory it draws the chariot of the Church. It is almost always read as Christ, one person with two natures: the eagle is the divine and the lion the human.

griffolino.name: Griffolino of Arezzo
griffolino.summary: An alchemist from Arezzo, known almost entirely from Dante and his early commentators. They say he tricked a rich and foolish young Sienese, Albero, with a promise to teach him to fly, and was burned as a heretic for it. Dante places him among the falsifiers in the last ditch of Malebolge.

guelphs-and-ghibellines.name: Guelphs and Ghibellines
guelphs-and-ghibellines.tagline: The warring parties of medieval Italy
guelphs-and-ghibellines.summary: Two parties that divided the Italian cities in the 13th century. In broad terms the Guelphs sided with the pope and the Ghibellines with the Holy Roman Emperor, though local family feuds counted for as much. Florence ended up firmly Guelph. Around 1300 its Guelphs split into Whites and Blacks, and Dante, a White, was exiled when the Blacks took power.

guido-cavalcanti.name: Guido Cavalcanti
guido-cavalcanti.summary: The leading Florentine poet of the generation before Dante's fame, and the man Dante called his first friend. His love poems are philosophical and dark, and he had a name for proud solitude and unbelief. He died in August 1300, a few months after the date of Dante's journey. Dante weighs his fame again in Purgatorio 11.

guido-da-montefeltro.name: Guido da Montefeltro
guido-da-montefeltro.summary: Lord of Urbino and the ablest Italian commander of his day, famous for his cunning. Late in life he made peace with the Church and in 1296 became a Franciscan friar. Dante praised him in an earlier work, the Convivio, but in Inferno 27 puts him among the counsellors of fraud. His son Buonconte appears in Purgatorio 5.

guido-del-duca.name: Guido del Duca
guido-del-duca.summary: A nobleman of the Onesti family of Ravenna who lived at Bertinoro and served as a judge in several towns of Romagna. He is recorded between 1199 and 1249. Dante places him among the envious in Purgatory, where he laments the decline of Tuscany and of Romagna.

guido-guerra.name: Guido Guerra
guido-guerra.summary: A nobleman of the powerful Conti Guidi family and one of the chief captains of the Guelph party in Tuscany. He led the exiled Florentine Guelphs who fought for Charles of Anjou at the battle of Benevento in 1266, the victory that brought their party back to power.

guido-guinizzelli.name: Guido Guinizzelli
guido-guinizzelli.summary: A poet of Bologna whose love poems, joining praise of the lady to ideas from philosophy, opened the way for what Dante calls the sweet new style. Dante meets him among the lustful in Purgatorio 26 and calls him his father in poetry.

guittone-d-arezzo.name: Guittone d'Arezzo
guittone-d-arezzo.summary: The most influential Italian poet of the generation before Dante, who wrote love poems and later moral and religious verse. Dante repeatedly judges his style to be rough and overpraised, and sets his own "sweet new style" against it.

hannibal.name: Hannibal
hannibal.summary: Commander of Carthage in its second war with Rome. He crossed the Alps into Italy with his army and elephants in 218 BC and won great victories, above all at Cannae, but could not take Rome. Scipio defeated him at Zama in North Africa in 202 BC.

harpies.name: The Harpies
harpies.summary: Birds with the faces of women, foul and ravenous. In Virgil's Aeneid they live on the Strophades, islands in the Ionian Sea, and befoul the food of Aeneas and his men. Dante sets them in the wood of the suicides, where they feed on the leaves of the trees.

heaven-of-jupiter.name: The Heaven of Jupiter
heaven-of-jupiter.summary: The sphere of the planet Jupiter, sixth of the nine heavens that turn around the earth. The souls of just rulers appear in it. They spell out a verse of Scripture in praise of justice, then form the figure of an eagle (Paradiso 18–20).

heaven-of-mars.name: The Heaven of Mars
heaven-of-mars.summary: The fifth of the nine heavens, glowing red like the planet. Here appear the souls of those who fought and died for the faith, as lights moving along a vast cross on which Christ flashes. The visit fills Paradiso 14–18.

heaven-of-mercury.name: The Heaven of Mercury
heaven-of-mercury.summary: The second of the planetary spheres that circle the earth in Dante's universe. Here he meets souls who did great good in the world, but partly for the sake of honor and fame. Like all the blessed they truly live with God in the Empyrean, and show themselves in this sphere only as a sign of their degree of bliss. Paradiso 5–7.

heaven-of-saturn.name: Saturn
heaven-of-saturn.summary: The seventh of the nine heavens that turn around the earth, and the last of the planets, above Jupiter and below the fixed stars. It is named for the god who ruled the Golden Age. In Paradiso 21–22 it shows Dante the contemplatives, souls who gave their lives to prayer and to thinking on God.

heaven-of-the-fixed-stars.name: The Fixed Stars
heaven-of-the-fixed-stars.summary: The sphere that carries all the stars and constellations, above the seven planets and below the Primum Mobile. The stars were called fixed because they keep their places relative to one another while the planets wander. Dante enters it in Gemini, his birth sign, and stays from Paradiso 22 to 27.

heaven-of-the-moon.name: The Moon
heaven-of-the-moon.summary: The lowest and slowest of the nine heavenly spheres, and the nearest to the earth. Because the moon waxes and wanes, it is linked with inconstancy, and here Dante meets souls who took religious vows and did not keep them. Like all the blessed they really dwell in the Empyrean, and only show themselves in this sphere.

heaven-of-the-sun.name: The Heaven of the Sun
heaven-of-the-sun.summary: The fourth of the planetary spheres that circle the earth in Dante's universe. Here he meets the souls of the wise: theologians, philosophers and teachers, who appear as rings of singing lights brighter than the sun itself. Like all the blessed they truly live with God in the Empyrean. Paradiso 10–14.

heaven-of-venus.name: The Heaven of Venus
heaven-of-venus.summary: The third of the planetary spheres that circle the earth in Dante's universe. Here he meets souls whose great capacity for love once ran to earthly passion and was turned in the end toward God. Like all the blessed they truly live with God in the Empyrean, and show themselves here only as a sign of their degree of bliss. Paradiso 8–9.

heavenly-spheres.name: The heavenly spheres
heavenly-spheres.summary: In the astronomy Dante learned, the earth stands still at the center of nine transparent spheres, nested one inside the next. The first seven each carry a planet: the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn. The eighth carries the fixed stars, and the ninth, the Primum Mobile, turns all the rest. Beyond them is the Empyrean. Dante rises through them in order, meeting the blessed in each.

hector.name: Hector
hector.summary: Troy's greatest warrior and the eldest son of King Priam, killed by Achilles outside the city walls in the Iliad. Medieval Europe admired him as a model of the noble knight.

helen.name: Helen of Troy
helen.summary: The wife of Menelaus, king of Sparta, and the most beautiful woman in the world in Greek legend. The Trojan prince Paris carried her off to Troy, and the Greeks fought for ten years to get her back.

hell.name: Hell
hell.tagline: The first realm of the journey
hell.summary: A vast funnel under Jerusalem, sinking in nine circles to the center of the earth, where Lucifer is frozen in ice. Each circle down is narrower and punishes worse sins, and each punishment mirrors its sin.

henry-vii.name: Henry VII
henry-vii.summary: Henry of Luxembourg, elected king of the Germans in 1308. He came to Italy in 1310 to restore the empire's authority and was crowned emperor in Rome in 1312. Dante greeted him as the savior of Italy, but Henry met resistance from Florence and the pope and died of fever in 1313. A throne waits for him in Paradiso 30.

heraclitus.name: Heraclitus
heraclitus.summary: The philosopher of change, who taught that everything is in flux and that you can't step into the same river twice. He believed fire was the root of all things.

hercules.name: Hercules
hercules.tagline: Hero of Greek and Roman myth
hercules.summary: The strongest of the ancient heroes, a son of Jupiter, famous for his twelve labors. The poem recalls several of his deeds: he dragged the dog Cerberus out of the underworld, killed the thief Cacus, wrestled the giant Antaeus, and set up the pillars that marked the western edge of the world.

hippocrates.name: Hippocrates
hippocrates.summary: The father of medicine, who taught that disease has natural causes, not divine ones. The doctors' oath still bears his name.

homer.name: Homer
homer.summary: The poet of the Iliad and the Odyssey, the first of epic poets in medieval esteem. Dante couldn't read Greek, so he knew Homer only by reputation and through Latin writers. His Ulysses, in Inferno 26, is largely his own invention.

honorius-iii.name: Honorius III
honorius-iii.summary: The successor of Innocent III. He formally approved the Dominican order in 1216 and confirmed the final rule of the Franciscans in 1223.

horace.name: Horace
horace.summary: Poet of the Odes, the Satires and the Art of Poetry, a guide to writing that medieval schools taught closely. Dante knew him mainly as a moralist and critic.

hugh-capet.name: Hugh Capet
hugh-capet.summary: The founder of the Capetian dynasty, which ruled France for centuries. He was the son of Hugh the Great, duke of the Franks, and was chosen king in 987 when the line of Charlemagne failed.

hugh-of-saint-victor.name: Hugh of Saint Victor
hugh-of-saint-victor.summary: A canon of the abbey of Saint Victor in Paris and the most famous teacher of its school. His writings on the sacraments, on study and on the contemplative life shaped the theology of the next two centuries.

hypsipyle.name: Hypsipyle
hypsipyle.summary: When the women of Lemnos killed all the men of the island, she alone spared her father, King Thoas, and got him away in secret. Jason became her lover and left her with twin sons. In the Thebaid of Statius she is later a slave and nurse in Greece, who shows a thirsty army the way to a spring.

icarus.name: Icarus
icarus.tagline: The boy who flew too near the sun
icarus.summary: Son of the craftsman Daedalus, who made wings of feathers and wax so the two could escape from Crete. Icarus ignored his father's warning and flew too high, the sun melted the wax, and he fell into the sea and drowned. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses.

innocent-iii.name: Innocent III
innocent-iii.summary: Lotario dei Conti di Segni, one of the most powerful popes of the Middle Ages. He gave Francis of Assisi and his first companions spoken approval for their way of life in 1209 or 1210.

jacob.name: Jacob
jacob.summary: Son of Isaac and grandson of Abraham. After wrestling with an angel he was renamed Israel, and his twelve sons became the twelve tribes of Israel.

jacobs-ladder.name: Jacob's ladder
jacobs-ladder.tagline: The stairway from earth to Heaven
jacobs-ladder.summary: In Genesis 28 the patriarch Jacob dreams of a ladder set on the earth with its top in heaven, and angels going up and down it. Monastic writers took it as a picture of the contemplative life, the soul's climb to God by humility and prayer. Dante sees it as a golden stairway rising from Saturn to the Empyrean.

jacopo-del-cassero.name: Jacopo del Cassero
jacopo-del-cassero.summary: A Guelph nobleman from Fano, on the Adriatic coast. As chief magistrate of Bologna in 1296 he made an enemy of Azzo VIII of Este, lord of Ferrara. Two years later, on his way to take up the same office in Milan, he was caught and killed by Azzo's men at Oriago, near Venice.

jacopo-rusticucci.name: Jacopo Rusticucci
jacopo-rusticucci.summary: A Florentine prominent in the city's affairs in the middle of the 1200s. Dante meets him in Inferno 16, running with Tegghiaio Aldobrandi among the sodomites.

james-the-greater.name: Saint James
james-the-greater.summary: One of the twelve apostles, son of Zebedee and brother of John. With Peter and John he was one of the three closest to Jesus. His shrine at Santiago de Compostela in Spain was among the great pilgrim destinations of the Middle Ages. In Paradiso 25 he examines Dante on hope.

jason.name: Jason
jason.summary: The Greek hero who sailed in the ship Argo to Colchis, on the Black Sea, to win the Golden Fleece. On the way he became the lover of Hypsipyle, queen of Lemnos, and left her. In Colchis the king's daughter Medea helped him take the Fleece and sailed away with him, and he later abandoned her too.

jerome.name: Jerome
jerome.summary: A priest and scholar who translated the Bible into Latin. His version, the Vulgate, was the Bible of the Middle Ages and the one Dante read. He is one of the four great Latin teachers of the church.

joachim-of-fiore.name: Joachim of Fiore
joachim-of-fiore.summary: A monk from Calabria, in the far south of Italy, who founded his own monastery at Fiore. He read the Bible as a prophecy of history in three ages, of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit, with the third, an age of peace and spiritual understanding, soon to come. His ideas were taken up by the strict wing of the Franciscans, and some of them were condemned.

john-chrysostom.name: John Chrysostom
john-chrysostom.summary: A Greek Father of the Church, called Chrysostom, "golden mouth", for his preaching. As archbishop of Constantinople he denounced the luxury of the imperial court and died in exile for it.

john-the-baptist.name: John the Baptist
john-the-baptist.summary: The preacher in the desert who announced the coming of Christ and baptized him in the Jordan. He was beheaded by Herod. He is the patron saint of Florence: Dante was baptized in the church that bears his name, and the city's gold coin, the florin, carried his image.

john-the-evangelist.name: Saint John the Evangelist
john-the-evangelist.summary: One of the twelve apostles, called the disciple Jesus loved. The Middle Ages held him to be the author of the Gospel of John and of Revelation, the vision of the end of the world that closes the Bible. In Paradiso 25–26 he examines Dante on love.

john-xxii.name: John XXII
john-xxii.summary: Jacques Duèse, from Cahors in southern France, the second of the popes who ruled from Avignon. He was known for gathering money for the papal treasury. Dante, who wrote Paradiso during his reign, counts him among the ruinous popes.

joshua.name: Joshua
joshua.summary: The leader who took command of Israel after the death of Moses, crossed the Jordan, and conquered the Promised Land, beginning with Jericho. Dante sees him among the warriors of the faith in Paradiso 18.

judas.name: Judas
judas.summary: Judas Iscariot, one of the twelve apostles, who handed Christ over to his enemies for thirty pieces of silver and then hanged himself. For Dante he is the worst of all sinners. He is punished at the very bottom of Hell, in the mouth of Satan (Inferno 34).

judecca.name: Judecca
judecca.tagline: Fourth zone of the ninth circle
judecca.summary: The innermost ring of the frozen lake of Cocytus, around Lucifer himself, for those who betrayed their lords and benefactors. It is named for Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Christ. The souls here are wholly buried in the ice and cannot speak.

judith.name: Judith
judith.summary: A widow in the biblical Book of Judith. When the Assyrian general Holofernes besieged her city, she went into his camp, won his trust and cut off his head as he slept, and the leaderless army fled.

julia.name: Julia
julia.summary: Married to Pompey to seal his alliance with her father. Her death in childbirth in 54 BC helped bring the two men to civil war.

julius-caesar.name: Julius Caesar
julius-caesar.summary: The general whose victories in civil war ended the Roman Republic. Dante counts him as the first emperor and places him with the honored pagans of Limbo, while Brutus and Cassius, who murdered him, are chewed in Lucifer's mouths at the bottom of Hell.

jupiter.name: Jupiter
jupiter.summary: The chief god of the Romans, the Greek Zeus, also called Jove. He rules the sky and strikes down his enemies with the thunderbolt. Dante sometimes uses his name for the Christian God, and treats defiance of him as defiance of God.

justinian.name: Justinian
justinian.summary: Emperor at Constantinople, who had the whole of Roman law collected and put in order. His code was the basis of legal study in Dante's Italy. He speaks at length in Paradiso 6, telling the history of the Roman eagle.

lancelot.name: Lancelot
lancelot.summary: The best of King Arthur's knights in the French romances, and the lover of Arthur's queen, Guinevere. Their adultery helps bring Arthur's kingdom down.

latinus.name: King Latinus
latinus.tagline: King of Latium in the Aeneid
latinus.summary: The old king of central Italy who welcomed Aeneas and promised him his daughter's hand, which set off the war between the Trojans and the Italians.

lavinia.name: Lavinia
lavinia.summary: Promised first to Turnus and then to Aeneas, she became Aeneas's wife and the ancestor of the Romans. She appears again in Purgatorio 17, weeping for her mother, who killed herself in despair.

leah.name: Leah
leah.summary: In Genesis, the elder daughter of Laban and the sister of Rachel. Jacob was tricked into marrying her first, and she bore him many children. Medieval writers made her the figure of the active life, the life of good works, beside Rachel as the life of contemplation.

leopard.name: The leopard
leopard.summary: Dante's word, lonza, may mean a leopard, a lynx or a panther. The three beasts come from Jeremiah 5:6, where a lion, a wolf and a leopard punish a sinful people. The leopard is most often read as lust, or as fraud. Dante mentions it once more, in Inferno 16.

lethe.name: Lethe
lethe.summary: In classical myth the river of the underworld whose water makes the dead forget their past lives. Dante takes it out of Hell and puts it in the Earthly Paradise at the top of Mount Purgatory, where it washes away the memory of sin (Purgatorio 28 and 31).

limbo.name: Limbo
limbo.summary: From the Latin limbus, a hem or border. Medieval theologians placed unbaptized babies and the righteous of the Old Testament here. Dante adds the virtuous pagans of the ancient world, gives them a noble castle, and lets their only punishment be longing for a God they will never see.

lion.name: The lion
lion.summary: Usually read as pride, the root of all sin in medieval teaching, or as violence. Readers who take the three beasts politically make the lion the royal house of France.

lucan.name: Lucan
lucan.summary: Author of the Pharsalia, an epic of the civil war between Caesar and Pompey. Accused of plotting against Nero, he was forced to kill himself at 25. Dante draws on him often, especially for Cato, the guardian of Purgatory.

lucca.name: Lucca
lucca.summary: A walled city-republic in northwest Tuscany, between Florence and Pisa, grown rich on silk and banking. In Dante's time it was Guelph and usually allied with Florence against Pisa.

lucifer.name: Lucifer
lucifer.tagline: The fallen angel, king of Hell
lucifer.summary: The highest of the angels, who rebelled against God out of pride and was cast down from Heaven. Dante also calls him Satan, Beelzebub and Dis. He stands at the center of the earth, the lowest point of Hell, frozen to the chest in the ice of Cocytus.

lucretia.name: Lucretia
lucretia.summary: Raped by the king's son, she told her family and then killed herself. Her death roused the revolt that ended the Roman monarchy.

lucy.name: Saint Lucy (Lucia)
lucy.summary: A Sicilian saint put to death for her faith in the early 300s. Her name comes from the Latin for light, and she was prayed to for the health of the eyes. She helps Dante three times: here, in Purgatorio 9 where she carries him up the mountain as he sleeps, and from her seat in Heaven in Paradiso 32.

malacoda.name: Malacoda
malacoda.summary: "Evil Tail": the leader of the devils of the fifth ditch of Malebolge. He bargains with Virgil in Inferno 21, grants a safe conduct and assigns an escort of ten devils, while lying about the road ahead.

malebolge.name: Malebolge
malebolge.summary: The name means "evil pouches". It is a great sloping field of stone cut by ten ring-shaped ditches, each holding a different kind of fraud: seducers and pimps, flatterers, sellers of church offices, fortune-tellers, corrupt officials, hypocrites, thieves, false counselors, sowers of discord and falsifiers. Dante crosses it in Inferno 18–30.

malebranche.name: The Malebranche
malebranche.summary: "Evil Claws": the black, winged devils who guard the ditch of boiling pitch in Malebolge, where corrupt officials are punished. They carry hooks to push under any sinner who surfaces. Their dealings with Dante and Virgil fill Inferno 21–23, the most comic and coarse episode of the poem.

manfred.name: Manfred
manfred.summary: The illegitimate son of the emperor Frederick II, and king of Sicily and southern Italy from 1258. He led the Ghibelline cause in Italy and was excommunicated by more than one pope. The popes called in the French prince Charles of Anjou against him, and Manfred was killed fighting Charles at Benevento in 1266.

manto.name: Manto
manto.summary: A prophetess of Thebes in Greek myth. Roman poets brought her to Italy: in Virgil's Aeneid her son Ocnus founds Mantua, Virgil's home city, and names it after her.

mantua.name: Mantua
mantua.summary: Virgil was born in a village near Mantua, and the city honored him as its own. In Inferno 20 Virgil tells how it was founded, and in Purgatorio 6 a Mantuan poet, Sordello, embraces him on hearing the name.

marcia.name: Marcia
marcia.summary: The wife of Cato, Rome's model of stern virtue. In Purgatorio 1 Virgil appeals to Cato in her name, and Cato replies that she can move him no longer.

marco-lombardo.name: Marco Lombardo
marco-lombardo.summary: A man of the courts of northern Italy, remembered in early Italian story collections for his wisdom, his sharp tongue and his independence. Almost nothing certain is known of his life. "Lombardo" may mean that he came from Lombardy, or it may be a family name.

marcus-brutus.name: Marcus Brutus
marcus-brutus.summary: Marcus Junius Brutus, a Roman senator whom Julius Caesar had favored and forgiven. He led the conspiracy that stabbed Caesar to death in 44 BC, and killed himself two years later after his defeat at Philippi. He is a different man from the Brutus who founded the Roman Republic, whom Dante honors in Limbo.

mary.name: The Virgin Mary
mary.summary: For Dante the queen of Heaven and the greatest source of mercy for sinners. Her pity begins his rescue, scenes from her life are held up as examples on every terrace of Purgatory, and the poem ends with Saint Bernard's prayer to her in Paradiso 33.

matelda.name: Matelda
matelda.tagline: The lady of the Earthly Paradise
matelda.summary: The woman Dante finds singing and gathering flowers in the Garden of Eden. She explains the garden and leads souls through its two rivers. She is named only once, in Purgatorio 33, and who she is has never been settled. Early commentators thought of Countess Matilda of Tuscany (1046–1115). She is usually read as an image of human life in its first innocence.

matthew-of-acquasparta.name: Matthew of Acquasparta
matthew-of-acquasparta.summary: Head of the Franciscan order from 1287 and a cardinal from 1288, who allowed the rule of poverty to be loosely kept. Boniface VIII sent him to Florence as his envoy in 1300 and 1301, in the troubles that ended with Dante's exile.

medea.name: Medea
medea.summary: Daughter of the king of Colchis. She fell in love with Jason, used her magic to help him win the Golden Fleece, and fled with him to Greece. When he left her for another bride, she killed the bride and her own two children by Jason.

medusa.name: Medusa
medusa.summary: One of three monstrous sisters of Greek myth, with snakes for hair and a face that turned anyone who looked at it to stone. The hero Perseus cut off her head, watching only her reflection in his shield.

melissus.name: Melissus
melissus.summary: A philosopher from the island of Samos and a follower of Parmenides, who held that all that exists is one, infinite and unchanging. Aristotle used him as an example of crude argument.

michael.name: Michael
michael.summary: The leader of the angels of Heaven. In the Book of Revelation he fights the dragon, Satan, and casts him and his rebel angels out of Heaven (12:7–9).

michael-zanche.name: Michael Zanche
michael-zanche.summary: Michele Zanche, a powerful figure in Logudoro, the northwestern part of Sardinia. Little about him is certain; early commentators say he governed there in the time of King Enzo, son of the emperor Frederick II. He was murdered at a banquet by his son-in-law, Branca Doria of Genoa, whose punishment Dante describes in Inferno 33.

minos.name: Minos
minos.summary: A legendary king of Crete, son of Zeus and Europa, famous for his laws. Greek and Roman poets made him a judge of the dead. In Dante's Hell he stands at the entrance to the second circle, hears each soul's confession, and shows which circle it must go to by the number of times he wraps his tail around himself.

minotaur.name: The Minotaur
minotaur.summary: Half man and half bull, born to Pasiphae, queen of Crete, after she mated with a bull. King Minos shut him in the labyrinth and fed him on young Athenians sent as tribute, until Theseus killed him. Dante sets him at the head of the seventh circle, over the violent.

montaperti.name: Montaperti
montaperti.summary: A hill near Siena where, on 4 September 1260, the Ghibellines of Siena and the exiled Ghibellines of Florence, with German cavalry sent by King Manfred, destroyed the army of Guelph Florence. Thousands of Florentines died, and the Ghibellines ruled Florence for the next six years. The city never forgot the defeat.

mosca-dei-lamberti.name: Mosca dei Lamberti
mosca-dei-lamberti.summary: In the early 1200s he urged the murder of a young nobleman, Buondelmonte, who had jilted a bride. Florentines dated the feud between Guelphs and Ghibellines in their city from that killing. Dante meets him among the sowers of discord in Inferno 28.

moses.name: Moses
moses.summary: Who led Israel out of slavery in Egypt and received the Ten Commandments on Mount Sinai, giving his people their law.

muhammad.name: Mohammed
muhammad.tagline: Prophet and founder of Islam, about 570–632
muhammad.summary: The prophet of Islam, born in Mecca. Christians of the Middle Ages commonly misunderstood Islam as a breakaway from Christianity rather than a religion of its own, and legends even made its founder a renegade Christian. Dante's harsh treatment of him follows that view.

muses.name: The Muses
muses.summary: Nine sisters, daughters of Zeus and Memory, who inspired poetry, music and learning. Ancient poets began their epics by asking the Muses for help, and Dante keeps the custom, calling on them at the opening of Inferno and again of Purgatorio.

nathan.name: Nathan
nathan.summary: A prophet at the court of King David. When David took Bathsheba and had her husband killed, Nathan rebuked the king to his face (2 Samuel 12).

nessus.name: Nessus
nessus.summary: He tried to carry off Dejanira, the wife of Hercules, while ferrying her across a river, and Hercules shot him with a poisoned arrow. Dying, he gave her his blood as a supposed love charm. Years later she sent Hercules a robe smeared with it, and it burned him to death. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses.

nicholas-iii.name: Nicholas III
nicholas-iii.summary: Giovanni Gaetano Orsini, of one of the great noble families of Rome. He was an able politician, but notorious for nepotism: he gave church offices, lands and wealth to his relatives.

nimrod.name: Nimrod
nimrod.tagline: Builder of the Tower of Babel
nimrod.summary: In Genesis a king of Babel and "a mighty hunter before the Lord". The Bible does not call him a giant or name him as builder of the tower. Christian tradition, which Dante follows, did both, and blamed him for the confusion of tongues that followed. For Dante he is the great example of pride punished.

nino-visconti.name: Nino Visconti
nino-visconti.summary: Ugolino Visconti, known as Nino, a leader of the Guelphs of Pisa and ruler, with the title of judge, of Gallura in Sardinia. He was the grandson of Count Ugolino, with whom he shared and then disputed power in Pisa (Inferno 33). Driven out, he led the Tuscan Guelphs against his own city.

noah.name: Noah
noah.summary: The righteous man whom God spared, with his family and the animals, from the Flood that drowned the world (Genesis 6–9).

oderisi-da-gubbio.name: Oderisi da Gubbio
oderisi-da-gubbio.summary: A painter of illuminated manuscripts from Gubbio in Umbria, recorded working in Bologna around 1270. No surviving work can be given to him with certainty. In Purgatory he is among the proud, and speaks the poem's great lesson on how quickly fame passes.

old-man-of-crete.name: The Old Man of Crete
old-man-of-crete.tagline: Statue of the ages of mankind
old-man-of-crete.summary: A giant statue that Dante imagines standing inside Mount Ida in Crete: golden head, silver chest, brass belly, iron legs and one foot of clay. It joins the statue in King Nebuchadnezzar's dream in the Book of Daniel with Ovid's four ages of the world. It is an image of mankind's decline, and its tears feed the rivers of Hell.

omberto-aldobrandeschi.name: Omberto Aldobrandeschi
omberto-aldobrandeschi.summary: Son of Guglielmo Aldobrandeschi, of a great feudal family that held Santafiora and much of the Maremma in southern Tuscany. He fought the Sienese for years and was killed at his castle of Campagnatico in 1259. Dante places him among the proud in Purgatory.

orpheus.name: Orpheus
orpheus.summary: The poet of Greek myth whose music could move animals, trees and stones. He went down to the underworld to bring back his wife Eurydice, and lost her when he looked back.

ovid.name: Ovid
ovid.summary: Author of the Metamorphoses, a great book of myths of transformation and Dante's main source for classical mythology. Augustus banished him to the shores of the Black Sea, where he died in exile, as Dante would die in exile from Florence.

paolo-malatesta.name: Paolo Malatesta
paolo-malatesta.summary: A younger son of the lord of Rimini, and himself a married man. He was the lover of Francesca, his brother Gianciotto's wife, and Gianciotto killed them together. He held office in Florence in 1282, where the young Dante may have seen him.

paris.name: Paris
paris.summary: A son of Priam, king of Troy. He carried off Helen, the wife of the Greek king Menelaus, and so began the Trojan War, which ended with his own death and the burning of his city.

parmenides.name: Parmenides
parmenides.summary: A philosopher from Elea, a Greek city in southern Italy. He argued that all reality is one, unchanging thing, and that change and motion are illusions. Aristotle attacked his reasoning as faulty.

parnassus.name: Parnassus
parnassus.summary: A mountain in central Greece, above Delphi, sacred to Apollo and the Muses. The spring of Castalia on its slopes was said to give poetic inspiration. Poets name it to mean poetry itself.

pasiphae.name: Pasiphaë
pasiphae.tagline: Queen of Crete, mother of the Minotaur
pasiphae.summary: Wife of King Minos of Crete in Greek myth. She fell in love with a bull and had the craftsman Daedalus build a hollow wooden cow so that she could mate with it. Their child was the Minotaur, half man and half bull.

paul.name: Saint Paul
paul.summary: Saul of Tarsus, a persecutor of the first Christians who was converted by a vision on the road to Damascus and became the great missionary of the early Church. His letters make up much of the New Testament. He wrote of being caught up to the third heaven, which made him, with Aeneas, a forerunner of Dante's journey.

penthesilea.name: Penthesilea
penthesilea.summary: A warrior queen who came to fight for Troy after Hector's death and was killed by Achilles. Virgil pictures her leading her women into battle in the Aeneid.

peter.name: Saint Peter
peter.summary: A fisherman of Galilee and the chief of Christ's apostles, to whom Christ promised the keys of the kingdom of Heaven (Matthew 16). Tradition makes him the first bishop of Rome, so every pope is his successor. In Paradiso 24 he examines Dante on faith, and in Paradiso 27 he rages against the corrupt popes of Dante's day.

peter-comestor.name: Peter Comestor
peter-comestor.summary: Peter "the Eater", so called, it was said, because he devoured books. A teacher and chancellor at Paris, he wrote the Scholastic History, a retelling of the Bible's story that became a standard textbook.

peter-damian.name: Peter Damian
peter-damian.summary: Born in Ravenna, he became a monk and then prior of the hermitage of Fonte Avellana, known for its harsh rule. In 1057 he was made cardinal bishop of Ostia against his will. He wrote fiercely against the wealth and corruption of the clergy and worked to reform the Church. Dante meets him among the contemplatives in Paradiso 21.

peter-of-spain.name: Peter of Spain
peter-of-spain.summary: Author of the Summulae logicales, a handbook of logic in twelve books used in the schools for centuries. He has traditionally been identified with the Portuguese scholar who became Pope John XXI in 1276 and died the next year, though modern scholars doubt it.

phaethon.name: Phaethon
phaethon.summary: In Ovid's Metamorphoses, a boy who begged to drive the chariot of his father, the Sun, for one day. He could not hold the horses, the chariot ran wild and burned sky and earth, and Jupiter struck him down with a thunderbolt to save the world.

philip-the-fair.name: Philip the Fair
philip-the-fair.summary: Philip IV of France. He fought Pope Boniface VIII over the taxing of the clergy and sent the men who seized the pope at Anagni in 1303. Under the next pope but one, Clement V, the papacy moved to Avignon, and Philip destroyed the order of the Knights Templar. Dante attacks him repeatedly but never uses his name.

phlegethon.name: Phlegethon
phlegethon.summary: The river of fire in the classical underworld. In Dante it is a stream of boiling blood that rings the seventh circle, crosses the burning sand and falls into the pit below. Its name is not given until Inferno 14, where Virgil explains that all the rivers of Hell are one flow of water.

phlegyas.name: Phlegyas
phlegyas.summary: A king in Greek myth, son of the war god Mars. When Apollo seduced his daughter Coronis, he burned the god's temple at Delphi in a rage and was killed for it. In the Aeneid he sits in the underworld warning others to respect the gods. Dante makes him the ferryman of the marsh of the wrathful.

pia-de-tolomei.name: Pia
pia-de-tolomei.tagline: Sienese lady killed in the Maremma
pia-de-tolomei.summary: Known only from Purgatorio 5. The early commentators say she was of the Tolomei family of Siena and the wife of Nello dei Pannocchieschi, a lord in the Maremma, who had her killed at his castle there, out of jealousy or so that he could marry again. No document confirms the story.

piccarda-donati.name: Piccarda Donati
piccarda-donati.summary: Sister of Forese and Corso Donati. She became a nun of the order of Saint Clare, but her brother Corso took her from the convent by force and married her to a political ally. Dante meets her among the blessed in the heaven of the Moon (Paradiso 3).

pier-della-vigna.name: Pier della Vigna
pier-della-vigna.summary: A man of humble birth from Capua who rose to be chief minister and spokesman of the emperor Frederick II, and was also a poet and a famous writer of Latin letters. In 1249 he was accused of treason, arrested and blinded, and he is said to have killed himself in prison. Dante presents him as innocent of treason.

pisa.name: Pisa
pisa.summary: A city near the mouth of the Arno, in Dante's time a sea power and the chief Ghibelline city of Tuscany, the rival of Guelph Florence and Lucca. Its long decline began in 1284, when Genoa destroyed its fleet at the battle of Meloria.

pistoia.name: Pistoia
pistoia.summary: A city about twenty miles northwest of Florence, notorious in Dante's time for its bloody feuds. The split of the Guelphs into Blacks and Whites began there. Legend said it was founded by the survivors of the army of Catiline, the Roman conspirator.

plato.name: Plato
plato.summary: Socrates' student and Aristotle's teacher, who taught that the things we see are shadows of eternal forms. In Dante's day little of his work could be read in Latin besides part of the Timaeus.

plutus.name: Plutus
plutus.summary: The Greek god of wealth. He was often confused with Pluto, the god of the underworld, and Dante may have both in mind. In Hell he is a demon who guards the circle of the misers and the spendthrifts.

pompey.name: Pompey
pompey.summary: Pompey the Great, the leading Roman commander before Julius Caesar, at first Caesar's ally and son-in-law, then his rival. He led the Senate's side in the civil war, lost the battle of Pharsalus in 48 BC, and was murdered as he landed in Egypt. Lucan's poem on the civil war, which Dante knew well, tells his story.

primum-mobile.name: The Primum Mobile
primum-mobile.summary: The "first moved": the outermost sphere of the physical universe, with no star or planet in it. It spins fastest of all, out of longing for God, and passes its motion down to every sphere below. Dante enters it in Paradiso 27.

proserpina.name: Proserpina
proserpina.summary: Daughter of Ceres, goddess of the harvest. Pluto carried her off while she was gathering flowers and made her his queen. Her Greek name is Persephone. The ancients also identified her with the moon, as Dante does in Inferno 10, and he recalls her lost springtime in Purgatorio 28.

provenzan-salvani.name: Provenzan Salvani
provenzan-salvani.summary: The leading Ghibelline of Siena and in effect its master after the victory over Florence at Montaperti in 1260. In 1269 the Florentines defeated the Sienese at Colle di Val d'Elsa, took him prisoner and cut off his head. Dante places him among the proud in Purgatory.

ptolemy.name: Ptolemy
ptolemy.summary: Working in Alexandria, he set out the earth-centered universe of nested spheres that astronomers accepted until Copernicus. It is the universe Dante climbs through in the Paradiso.

ptolomea.name: Ptolomea
ptolomea.tagline: Third zone of the ninth circle
ptolomea.summary: The third ring of the frozen lake of Cocytus, for those who betrayed their guests. It is most likely named for Ptolemy, the governor of Jericho in the Bible, who invited his father-in-law Simon Maccabeus and two of his sons to a banquet and had them killed (1 Maccabees 16). Some think of the Egyptian king Ptolemy, who had Pompey murdered when he came seeking refuge.

purgatory.name: Purgatory
purgatory.tagline: The second realm of the journey
