purgatory.summary: A mountain on an island on the far side of the world, where saved souls are cleansed before Heaven. Its seven terraces purge the seven deadly sins, and the Garden of Eden waits at the top.

rabanus-maurus.name: Rabanus Maurus
rabanus-maurus.summary: Abbot of Fulda and later archbishop of Mainz, one of the most learned men of the age after Charlemagne. He wrote commentaries on much of the Bible and an encyclopedia.

rachel.name: Rachel
rachel.summary: Jacob worked seven years for her father to marry her, was tricked into marrying her sister Leah, and worked seven more (Genesis 29). Dante makes her the image of the contemplative life, and seats her beside Beatrice in Paradiso 32.

rahab.name: Rahab
rahab.summary: A prostitute of Jericho who hid the spies Joshua sent into the city and helped them escape. When Jericho fell she and her family alone were spared (Joshua 2 and 6). The New Testament praises her faith and names her among the ancestors of Christ.

rebecca.name: Rebecca
rebecca.summary: The wife of Isaac in Genesis and the mother of the twins Esau and Jacob. She helped Jacob, the younger, win the blessing his father meant for Esau.

rinieri-da-calboli.name: Rinieri da Calboli
rinieri-da-calboli.summary: Head of a leading Guelph family of Forlì in Romagna, who served as chief magistrate of several cities. He was killed in 1296 in the fighting for control of Forlì. Dante places him among the envious in Purgatory.

robert-of-anjou.name: Robert of Anjou
robert-of-anjou.summary: A younger son of Charles II of Anjou, who succeeded him as king of Naples and became the leader of the Guelphs in Italy and the chief opponent of Emperor Henry VII, in whom Dante placed his hopes. He was known as Robert the Wise and wrote many sermons, which Dante did not count in his favor.

roland.name: Roland
roland.summary: Hero of the Old French epic the Song of Roland. He commanded the rear guard of Charlemagne's army, which was ambushed and destroyed at Roncesvalles in the Pyrenees in 778. In the poem he is betrayed by Ganelon and is too proud to sound his horn for help until it is too late. Dante places him in Heaven beside Charlemagne.

romagna.name: Romagna
romagna.summary: The land between the Apennines and the Adriatic, south of the river Po, with the cities of Ravenna, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Cesena and Rimini. In Dante's time each city was held or fought over by a local lord. Dante spent his last years there, in Ravenna.

roman-eagle.name: The Roman eagle
roman-eagle.summary: The eagle, bird of Jupiter, was carried on the standards of the Roman legions. For Dante it stands for the Empire itself, the one worldly power that he believed God had appointed to give the world law and peace, as the Church was appointed to guide souls. In Paradiso 18–20 the souls of just rulers form a great eagle that speaks with one voice.

romeo-of-villeneuve.name: Romeo of Villeneuve
romeo-of-villeneuve.tagline: Minister of the count of Provence, died 1250
romeo-of-villeneuve.summary: Romieu de Villeneuve, chief minister of Raymond Berenger, count of Provence. Legend, which Dante follows, made him a humble pilgrim who arrived at the court from nowhere, made the count's fortune, was slandered by jealous courtiers, and left as poor as he came.

rudolf-of-habsburg.name: Rudolf of Habsburg
rudolf-of-habsburg.summary: Rudolf I, the first Habsburg to be elected emperor. He spent his reign securing his family's power in Germany and Austria and never went to Italy to be crowned. Dante blames him for leaving Italy without a ruler.

ruggieri-degli-ubaldini.name: Archbishop Ruggieri
ruggieri-degli-ubaldini.summary: Ruggieri degli Ubaldini, archbishop of Pisa from 1278 and leader of the city's Ghibellines. He pretended to ally with Count Ugolino, then raised the city against him and had him imprisoned and starved to death along with his sons and grandsons.

ruth.name: Ruth
ruth.summary: A woman of Moab in the biblical Book of Ruth. Left a widow, she stayed loyal to her Hebrew mother-in-law Naomi, followed her to Bethlehem and married Boaz there. King David was her great-grandson.

sabellius.name: Sabellius
sabellius.summary: A Christian teacher who denied that the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit are three distinct Persons. For him they were only three names or roles of a single God. The Church condemned the teaching.

saladin.name: Saladin
saladin.summary: The Muslim ruler who took Jerusalem back from the Crusaders in 1187. Even his Christian enemies admired him for his honor and generosity, and medieval Europe told stories of his chivalry.

sapia.name: Sapia
sapia.summary: A noblewoman of Siena, aunt of the city's ruler Provenzan Salvani and wife of Ghinibaldo Saracini, lord of a castle near the city. Dante places her among the envious in Purgatory, where she confesses that she rejoiced when her own townsmen were defeated at Colle di Val d'Elsa in 1269.

sarah.name: Sarah
sarah.summary: The wife of Abraham in Genesis, childless until old age, when she bore Isaac as God had promised. Through Isaac she is the mother of the people of Israel.

scipio-africanus.name: Scipio Africanus
scipio-africanus.summary: The general who ended the long war between Rome and Carthage by defeating Hannibal at Zama in North Africa in 202 BC. The victory earned him the name Africanus. For Dante he is one of the heroes through whom providence prepared Rome to rule the world.

semele.name: Semele
semele.summary: A daughter of Cadmus, the founder of Thebes, and the mother of Bacchus. Jupiter loved her, and jealous Juno tricked her into asking him to come to her in his full glory as a god. The sight burned her to ash. Ovid tells the story in the Metamorphoses.

semiramis.name: Semiramis
semiramis.summary: The wife and successor of King Ninus, credited in legend with great conquests and with building the walls of Babylon. Ancient and medieval writers made her a byword for lust.

seneca.name: Seneca
seneca.summary: Stoic philosopher and tutor to the young Nero, who later ordered his death. Medieval readers prized his letters on how to live.

seraphim.name: Seraphim
seraphim.summary: The first of the nine orders of angels, the ones nearest to God, who burn with the most love. The prophet Isaiah saw them around God's throne, each with six wings. In Dante's universe they turn the outermost moving sphere, the Primum Mobile, from which all the other heavens take their motion.

shade.name: Shade
shade.summary: Dante's word for the souls he meets. Their bodies are made of air: they speak, weep and suffer, but cast no shadow and can't be held. In Purgatorio 2, Dante tries three times to embrace a friend and closes his arms on nothing.

she-wolf.name: The she-wolf
she-wolf.summary: The beast that finally drives Dante back: greed, the endless craving for more that he blames for the corruption of Church and state. She returns throughout the poem, as the "cursed wolf" of Inferno 7 and the "ancient she-wolf" of Purgatorio 20.

siena.name: Siena
siena.summary: A hill city south of Florence and its great rival. Under Ghibelline rule it crushed the Florentines at Montaperti in 1260, then lost to them at Colle di Val d'Elsa in 1269. Dante's Florentine characters like to mock the Sienese as vain.

siger-of-brabant.name: Siger of Brabant
siger-of-brabant.summary: A master at the University of Paris who taught Aristotle as read by Averroes, including views that clashed with Christian doctrine, such as the eternity of the world. Thomas Aquinas wrote against him, the Church condemned such teachings, and he died at the papal court at Orvieto, reportedly stabbed by a clerk who had gone mad.

simon-magus.name: Simon Magus
simon-magus.tagline: Sorcerer in the Acts of the Apostles
simon-magus.summary: A magician of Samaria who was baptized and then offered the apostles Peter and John money for the power to confer the Holy Spirit. Peter answered, "May your silver perish with you" (Acts 8:9–24). The sin of buying or selling holy things is called simony after him.

sirens.name: The Sirens
sirens.tagline: Singers who lure sailors to their deaths
sirens.summary: In Greek myth, creatures whose song drew sailors onto the rocks. In Homer's Odyssey, Ulysses has himself tied to the mast so that he can hear them and live. For Dante they stand for pleasures that charm and destroy. He dreams of a Siren in Purgatorio 19.

socrates.name: Socrates
socrates.summary: The Athenian teacher who wrote nothing and questioned everything, and was sentenced to death for corrupting the young. Dante knew him only through other writers.

solomon.name: Solomon
solomon.summary: Son of David and builder of the Temple in Jerusalem. He asked God for wisdom to rule well and was given more than any other king. The Bible's books of Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and the Song of Songs were credited to him. Because he turned to foreign gods in old age, medieval theologians argued over whether he was saved.

sordello.name: Sordello
sordello.summary: A poet born at Goito, near Mantua, who spent most of his life at the courts of Provence and wrote in Provençal, the language of the troubadours. His best-known poem is a lament for a dead lord that rebukes the kings of Europe for cowardice. In the Comedy he guides Dante and Virgil through the lower slopes of Purgatory.

statius.name: Statius
statius.summary: Publius Papinius Statius, author of the Thebaid, an epic on the war of the Seven against Thebes, and the unfinished Achilleid. The Middle Ages ranked him among the greatest Latin poets. Dante makes him a secret Christian, converted by reading Virgil, and has him join Dante and Virgil on the upper terraces of Purgatory.

styx.name: Styx
styx.tagline: The marsh of the fifth circle
styx.summary: One of the rivers of the underworld in Greek and Roman myth. In Dante's Hell it is a dark swamp where the wrathful are punished. It surrounds the walls of the city of Dis, and Dante crosses it by boat in Inferno 8.

tarquin.name: Tarquin
tarquin.summary: Tarquinius Superbus, "the Proud", whose tyranny ended when his son raped Lucretia and the outraged Romans drove the family out.

tegghiaio-aldobrandi.name: Tegghiaio Aldobrandi
tegghiaio-aldobrandi.summary: A respected knight of the Adimari family in the generation before Dante's. He advised Florence against the campaign that ended in its defeat at Montaperti in 1260. Dante meets him among the sodomites in Inferno 16.

thales.name: Thales
thales.summary: Thales of Miletus, often called the first philosopher. He held that everything is made from water, and is said to have predicted an eclipse.

thebes.name: Thebes
thebes.summary: The city of Oedipus and his warring sons, in Greek legend a place of family murder, madness and civil war. Dante knew its story mainly from the Thebaid of Statius, and it is his standing example of a city cursed by its own crimes.

theological-virtues.name: The theological virtues
theological-virtues.summary: The three virtues that Christian teaching says come only as a gift of God and lead the soul to him. Saint Paul names them together and calls charity, or love, the greatest. Their traditional colors are white for faith, green for hope and red for charity.

theseus.name: Theseus
theseus.summary: The hero who killed the Minotaur in the labyrinth of Crete, with the help of the king's daughter Ariadne. Later he went down to the underworld with his friend Pirithous, who wanted to carry off its queen, and was held prisoner there.

thomas-aquinas.name: Thomas Aquinas
thomas-aquinas.summary: A Dominican friar from southern Italy and the greatest theologian of the Middle Ages. His Summa Theologiae joined Christian teaching to the philosophy of Aristotle, and much of the Comedy's thought follows him. In Paradiso he speaks at length among the wise in the Heaven of the Sun.

tiresias.name: Tiresias
tiresias.summary: The most famous prophet of Greek myth, who advised the kings of Thebes. Ovid tells that he was changed into a woman for seven years and then back into a man, and that he was struck blind and given the gift of prophecy in return. He is the father of the seer Manto.

titus.name: Titus
titus.summary: Son of the emperor Vespasian. As his father's general he captured Jerusalem in AD 70 and destroyed its Temple, and he later ruled as emperor for two years. Medieval Christians saw the fall of Jerusalem as vengeance for the death of Christ.

trajan.name: Trajan
trajan.summary: One of the most admired of the Roman emperors, remembered in the Middle Ages as a model of justice. Legend said that, centuries after his death, the prayers of Pope Gregory the Great brought him back to life long enough to believe and be saved. Dante sees him in Heaven among the just rulers (Paradiso 20).

trinity.name: The Trinity
trinity.summary: The Christian teaching that the one God is three Persons: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit. Medieval theologians often matched them with Power, Wisdom and Love, and Dante uses those names throughout the poem. The Son is also called the Word, who took on human nature as Christ.

tristan.name: Tristan
tristan.summary: The hero of one of the most popular love stories of the Middle Ages. A knight of Cornwall, he fell in love with Isolde, the wife of his uncle King Mark, and the love cost both of them their lives.

ubertino-da-casale.name: Ubertino da Casale
ubertino-da-casale.summary: A leader of the Spirituals, the Franciscans who demanded that the rule of poverty be kept to the letter. He attacked the laxity of the order and of the popes in his book The Tree of the Crucified Life of Jesus.

ugolino.name: Count Ugolino
ugolino.summary: Ugolino della Gherardesca, a powerful count who came from a Ghibelline family but allied himself with the Guelphs and for a time ruled Pisa. In 1288 his rival Archbishop Ruggieri turned the city against him, and he was shut in a tower with two sons and two grandsons and left to starve. Dante places him in the ice among the traitors to their country, gnawing forever on the archbishop's head (Inferno 32–33).

ulysses.name: Ulysses
ulysses.tagline: Greek hero of the Trojan War
ulysses.summary: The Latin name of Odysseus, king of Ithaca, the cleverest of the Greeks at Troy and the hero of Homer's Odyssey. Dante could not read Homer. He knew Ulysses from Latin writers, above all Virgil, who show him as a schemer and deceiver. He burns in the eighth ditch of Malebolge in Inferno 26, where Dante gives him a last voyage of his own invention.

valley-of-the-princes.name: Valley of the Princes
valley-of-the-princes.summary: A sheltered dell on the mountainside, bright with flowers, where kings and lords wait to enter Purgatory. They were so taken up with ruling, or with failing to rule, that they neglected their souls until late. Dante spends his first night on the mountain here (Purgatorio 7–8).

vanni-fucci.name: Vanni Fucci
vanni-fucci.summary: The illegitimate son of a nobleman of Pistoia, known as a violent partisan of the Black Guelphs. In 1293 he took part in robbing the treasury of the chapel of San Jacopo in Pistoia's cathedral. Dante puts him among the thieves in Inferno 24–25, the most defiant soul in Hell.

venus.name: Venus
venus.summary: The Roman goddess of love and the mother of Cupid. Her planet is the bright morning and evening star, and in the astronomy of Dante's time it was thought to incline people to love. Dante sometimes calls her Cytherea, after the island of Cythera, where she was said to have risen from the sea.

virgil.name: Virgil
virgil.summary: Author of the Aeneid, the epic of Rome's founding, and Dante's guide through Hell and up the mountain of Purgatory. For Dante he stands for the best that human reason and art can reach without Christian faith. Medieval readers also honored him as an unknowing prophet of Christ, because of a prophecy of a wondrous child in his Fourth Eclogue.

xerxes.name: Xerxes
xerxes.summary: The Persian king who invaded Greece in 480 BC with a huge army, crossing from Asia into Europe on a bridge of boats. The Greeks defeated his fleet at Salamis and he went home in retreat. For ancient and medieval writers he was a standard example of pride brought low.

zeno.name: Zeno
zeno.summary: Most likely Zeno of Citium (c. 334–262 BC), founder of the Stoics, who taught that virtue is the only good. Possibly Zeno of Elea, known for his paradoxes about motion.
